replies.user: [BASICS: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what an AI chatbot is, in plain words. Keep it short, then let me try one.
replies.raw:
Welcome. I'm Merc, a chatbot in a learning app built to help you get comfortable with AI.

You can't break anything here, and there are no silly questions. If something goes wrong, we start again.

Type in the box at the bottom, or tap the microphone on your keyboard and talk. Then tap the arrow to send.

An AI chatbot is a computer program you talk to by typing or speaking. It writes back in plain words.

No one is typing back to you — it's all the computer.

There are many chatbots out there: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot. Merc is one too.

What you learn here works in all of them.

Try asking me: "Are you a real person?"

replies.user: Are you a real person?
replies.raw:
No. I'm Merc, a chatbot in a learning app. No one is typing back to you.

Practicing on me works the same way as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Copilot.

Notice that you got a straight answer right away. That's one thing chatbots are good at.

Now ask me anything you're curious about. It can be about cooking, your garden, or a place you'd like to visit.

replies.user: How do I keep basil alive on a windowsill?
replies.raw:
Basil loves sun, so a south-facing window is best. It needs at least six hours of light a day.

Water it when the top of the soil feels dry. Don't let it sit in water, or the roots will rot.

Pinch off any flowers as soon as you see them. That keeps the leaves coming.

[KEY]A chatbot learned from a huge amount of writing, and it makes each answer by guessing, word by word, what fits best.[/KEY]

It isn't a person, and it isn't a search engine. It doesn't look your question up — it builds the answer word by word, based on everything it learned.

Notice how you asked about your own basil on your own windowsill, and got a specific, useful answer. That's how to get good help from a chatbot.

Tap the answer you think is right. There's no grade.

[Q]
Which is the best description of an AI chatbot?
A) A person at the company typing answers to you
B) A computer program that writes answers by guessing what words fit best
C) A big library of facts that looks up the right answer every time
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) A computer program that writes answers by guessing what words fit best
replies.raw:
That's exactly right.

You asked about your own basil, and that's how to get good help from a chatbot.

One thing to keep in mind: if you wouldn't write something on a postcard for anyone to read, don't type it into a chatbot.

replies.user: [BASICS: Unit 2, Lesson 3] Teach me what I should never share with an AI chatbot, and why. Then let me practice asking for help safely.
replies.raw:
Last time, you asked a chatbot to say something in plain words.

Some things are safe to share with a chatbot. Others are not.

Here is what to **never** type into a chatbot:

- Passwords and PINs
- One-time codes (the code a company texts you to log in)
- Bank or card numbers
- Social Security, Medicare or other ID numbers
- Medical records
- Photos of your ID, Medicare or insurance card
- Other people's private details

A general detail, like "I'm allergic to nuts", is fine. You can almost always get good help without the private part.

Try asking me: "My bank charged me twice. What should I do?"

replies.user: My bank charged me twice. What should I do?
replies.raw:
Here are some steps to take:

1. Check your statement to confirm the double charge is there.
2. Call your bank using the number on the back of your card or on your statement.
3. Tell them the date, the amount, and the name of the merchant.
4. Ask them to reverse the extra charge. Most banks do this quickly once you report it.

Notice that you didn't need your account number to get good help.

Your chats are usually saved, and some companies use them to improve their AI. To control this, look for the settings or privacy option in any chatbot app, or use a temporary chat.

The safest step is to leave private details out in the first place.

[KEY]You can almost always get good help without typing private details.[/KEY]

[Q]
Which one is safe to type into a chatbot?
A) "Is Rosebud1952 a strong password?"
B) "How do I make a strong password I can remember?"
C) The code your bank texted you a minute ago, so it can explain it
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) "How do I make a strong password I can remember?"
replies.raw:
You kept the question general, and that's exactly right.

Option A shares an actual password, even as an example. Option C shares a live security code, which is meant for one use only.

Neither one needed to be typed.

You already know the key rule: if you wouldn't write it on a postcard, don't type it into a chatbot.

Next time you ask a chatbot for help, leave out names and numbers, and see if the help is still good.

Try this today: Next time you ask a chatbot for help, leave out names and numbers, and see if the help is still good.

replies.user: [BASICS: Unit 2, Lesson 4] Teach me about AI voice-clone and family emergency scams, and exactly what to do if I get one of those calls. Then help me make a plan.
replies.raw:
Last time, you learned the postcard rule.

AI can copy someone's voice from a short recording — even a video posted online. Scammers use that to call you sounding exactly like a grandchild or other relative.

Even if the name or number shows on your screen, callers can fake that too.

The warning signs come fast:

- It's urgent.
- It's a secret ("don't tell Mom").
- They want cash, gift cards, or a wire transfer.
- Sometimes someone comes to your door to pick up the money.

[KEY]If a caller sounds like family but asks for money in secret, that's a scam.[/KEY]

[EX]In 2023, an Arizona mother got a call. Her 15-year-old daughter was safe the whole time. But a voice that sounded exactly like her daughter asked for help, and a man demanded money. The mother later told the U.S. Senate about it.[/EX]

A code word is a word only your family knows. If a caller can't say it, hang up.

Try asking me: "Write a text asking my family to pick a code word."

replies.user: Write a text asking my family to pick a code word.
replies.raw:
Here's a text you could send:

---

"Hey everyone — I just learned about a scam where AI can fake someone's voice to sound like family. One way to protect ourselves is a code word. If anyone ever calls saying they're in trouble, they say the word and we know it's really them.

Can we pick one together? Love you all."

---

Notice how it explains the reason, so your family will take it seriously.

Now try: "Make it short and friendly."

replies.user: Make it short and friendly.
replies.raw:
Here's a shorter version:

---

"Hey family! Can we pick a secret code word? If anyone calls saying they're in trouble, they say the word so we know it's really them. It's a quick way to protect each other.

Love you!"

---

Don't tell me the actual code word. Keep that for your family.

Now, one thing to know about what to do when a call comes in.

**Hang up and call back.** Call the person on a number you already know — from your contacts, or a number you've dialed before.

If you can't reach them, call another family member, even if the caller said to keep it secret.

Hanging up won't hurt them. If it's real, they'll still be okay in the five minutes it takes to check.

[Q]
A call sounds exactly like your grandson. He's crying, says he's in jail, and asks you to buy gift cards and keep it secret. What do you do first?
A) Buy the gift cards so he's safe
B) Hang up and call him, or his parents, on a number you already know
C) Ask the caller for a phone number to call him back
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) Hang up and call him, or his parents, on a number you already know
replies.raw:
That's exactly right.

You spotted the key move: hang up first, then call back on a number you already know. Option C is the trap — any number the scammer gives you goes right back to them.

You wrote a text your family will actually want to read, and that's how this protection works in real life.

Send the code-word text to your family today.

replies.user: How do I keep basil alive on a windowsill?
replies.raw:
Great question. Here's what basil needs to thrive on a windowsill:

**Light:** Basil loves sun. A south- or west-facing window is best.

It needs at least 6 hours of light a day.

**Water:** Stick your finger about an inch into the soil. If it feels dry, water it.

If it still feels damp, wait. Basil hates sitting in soggy soil, so make sure the pot drains.

**Heat:** Basil likes warmth. Keep it away from cold drafts and air conditioning vents.

**Pinching:** When you see flower buds forming, pinch them off. This keeps the plant bushy and the leaves tasty.

Notice how asking about your own basil got you a specific, useful answer.

A chatbot learned from a huge amount of writing. It makes each answer by guessing, word by word, what fits best.

It isn't a person, and it isn't a search engine. There are many: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot.

What you learn here works in all of them.

Tap the answer you think is right. There's no grade.

replies.user: What does this mean, and what do I need to do?
replies.raw:
Here's what this letter is saying:

Your plan is raising the amount you pay for certain drugs before the plan starts helping. That amount is called a **deductible** — it's the total you pay each year before the plan pays its share.

Right now that amount is $250. Starting January 1, it goes up to $400.

After you hit that $400, you'll pay 25% of the cost of specialty-tier drugs. Those are the most expensive kind of drugs a plan covers.

As for what to do: nothing, unless you want to switch to a different plan.

---

Notice how asking "what do I need to do?" got you a clear action, not only an explanation.

Now try: "By when?"

replies.user: By when?
replies.raw:
If you want to switch plans, you'd need to do it by December 7 — that's the end of the Annual Enrollment Period.

Some people can switch at other times too. Your state's free Medicare helpers, called SHIP, can tell you what applies to you.

If you're happy with your plan, you don't need to do anything at all.

---

One more thing before you use this with a real letter: always call the sender yourself to confirm anything about money or benefits. Use the number on your card or a past bill — not a number from a surprise letter or email.
